source.title: Double Double Descent: On Generalization Errors in Transfer Learning between Linear Regression Tasks

record.tranche_reason: The study analytically and empirically examines double descent in Gaussian linear regression transfer learning, a different model class and setting from the deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: The study's own results on target-task generalization error versus free-parameter counts are included. Claims about deep networks and double descent from cited work, and the source-task double-descent result described as available from prior work, are not recorded as findings here. The paper does not sweep training sample size.
record.test_reason: The paper derives and simulates target-task test error against free-parameter count in Gaussian linear-regression transfer learning. This is a new setting with direct results on the second descent past interpolation (V4) and on peak removal by tuned ridge (V6). It is a new setting rather than a different method on the same question, so T3 fits better than the reader's T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The paraphrase should add that the authors stress how fragile beneficial transfer is (it depends on the transferred set, the task relation and the true β). They also show that a source task closer or identical to the target is not necessarily optimal when overparameterized.
record.recipe_differences: Analytical and empirical transfer learning between Gaussian linear-regression tasks, including minimum-norm and ridge solutions; not the original deep-network model-size experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The results depend on the transfer layout and count, source-target relation H, true parameter structure β, task-relation noise, and regularization tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Whether parameter transfer beats zeroed or free parameters depends on the source-task parameterization, the task-relation noise and the H operator (Figs. 5–7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In transfer learning, benefits of parameter transfer rise as the source task becomes more overparameterized.

record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The tested setting is Gaussian linear regression with synthetic experiments. Many empirical curve values are shown only in figures; the paper does not sweep target sample size or training epochs. The study itself notes that some curves lack a first descent and that its minimum-ℓ1 experiments do not clearly show an additional peak.
record.rows_left_out: No further related empirical curves were left out; cited results from other work and source-task double descent attributed to prior work were excluded.

untested.parts: No sweep over training sample size n.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs and samples.
The paper does not test whether label noise drives the peak; the noise level is not swept against peak height.

missing.what: Near maximal overparameterization, the minimum-l2 interpolator performs comparably to tuned ridge, i.e. interpolation substitutes for regularization.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this paper. The double descent here is largely 'without the first descent' because of arbitrary coordinate selection, which the authors acknowledge. The source-task double descent is taken from prior work (Belkin, Hsu, Xu) and is correctly excluded from the rows. The task-relation noise ση² is varied but not tested as the driver of the peak.

versions.untested_parts: Changing the number of target-task training examples near interpolation.
The study tests Gaussian linear regression, not a broad range of model classes; it does not establish that every curve includes a first descent or subsumes the classical U-shaped curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

The paper tests approximately tuned and suboptimally tuned ridge regularization, and reports on additional peaks for minimum-ℓ1 solutions. It does not establish that label noise or variance drives the peak; the sample-size and epoch axes are not tested.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameter number or conversion of the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Target task linear regression (minimum ℓ2-norm solution)
rows.operation_detail: Analytically characterize target-task out-of-sample error as p varies
rows.value: Theorem 3.1: error is infinite for n−1 ≤ p ≤ n+1; for p ≥ n+2 it is (p−1)/(p−n−1) times (||β_Z||² + σ²_ε + E_transfer) plus (p−n)/p ||β_F||². The authors state that the error peaks around p=n and decreases in the overparameterized range.
rows.note: The stated result is for target-task generalization in the paper's transfer-learning setup; E_transfer depends on the source task and transferred coordinates.

rows.subject: Target task linear regression (minimum ℓ2-norm solution)
rows.operation_detail: Empirically evaluate generalization error while varying p
rows.note: The text says the error peaks at p=n and then decreases for p>n+1 across the plotted cases.
rows.check: Sec. 3.2 states these Fig. 1 curves are double descent 'without the first descent'. The second descent past p=n+1 is observed, but there is no U-shaped underparameterized part, so 'observed' overstates the fit.

rows.subject: Target task linear regression (ridge regression)
rows.operation_detail: Empirically evaluate approximately optimally tuned ridge regression across parameterization levels
rows.measure: Target-task out-of-sample error and presence of a double-descent peak
rows.baseline: interpolating minimum ℓ2- and minimum ℓ1-norm solutions
rows.value: The authors state that approximately optimally tuned ridge resolves the error peak and eliminates the double-descent shape; plotted numerical values are figure only.
rows.note: This is a regularized, non-interpolating solution; it tests the regularization-dependence part of V6.

rows.subject: Target task linear regression (ridge regression)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate ridge regression with suboptimal regularization settings

conditions.value: α and α̃ are κ times their approximately optimal values

rows.measure: Target-task out-of-sample error and residual peak
rows.baseline: approximately optimally tuned ridge and interpolating solutions
rows.value: The authors state that suboptimal tuning may not fully resolve the double-descent peak; plotted numerical values are figure only.
rows.note: This shows dependence of peak removal on regularization tuning.
rows.check: A residual peak under suboptimal tuning (kappa times the approximately optimal alpha) is consistent with V6, which claims removal only under optimal tuning. It is not a partial effect.

rows.subject: Target task linear regression (minimum ℓ1-norm interpolator)
rows.operation_detail: Assess whether the minimum-ℓ1 error curves show an additional overparameterized peak

rows.value: The authors say they do not clearly observe an additional peak in the overparameterized range.
rows.note: The authors suggest the predetermined-coordinate misspecification strategy could explain the lack of a clearly observed extra peak.
rows.check: The authors report no clearly observed additional peak for minimum-l1. That is absence of the multiple-descent part of V6 in this setting, not a partial effect.

relationships.condition: Minimum-l2 and minimum-l1 interpolating linear regression in transfer learning, along both the target (p) and source (p̃) parameter axes
relationships.reason: Error peaks at p=n (and at p̃=ñ when t>0) and decreases through the overparameterized range, analytically and empirically (R1, R10–R13).
relationships.display_finding: Error peaked at p=n and, with transferred parameters, at p̃=ñ before declining; minimum-ℓ1 experiments demonstrated target-capacity recovery, while some target curves lacked an initial descent and extensive transfer restricted accessible ranges.
